author: @paullasky6865

text:
Framerate doesnt equal hertz.

It has the power to render over 120 frames at native 4K in certain games, but the display interface isn't capable of displaying 120hz.

You can play at 120fps in 60hz just like you can play at 200fps in 480p , just because your monitor is a certain refresh rate doesnt mean that you cant render more than that, you just wont actually see those extra frames with your eyeballs, you're only locked to your refresh rate if you're using Vertical Syncronization.

author: @paullasky6865

text:
@paullasky6865  
Ask away, no problem, your questions don't bother.

Depending on your ram, it could be fine, the mighty 9900K is still stronger than an i3 12100F but weaker than an i5 12400F.

Though if im being honest, perhaps the 4090 is too strong to the point that even at 4K, your cpu might limit it, also when we begin to factor in the fact that you're limited to PCI-E 3.0 , it's a tough call.

If you have a 3090 though, you should be able to sell it instantly for 800, maybe even 900, and then the 4090 doesn't become such a brutally expensive product, if you sell your 3090 for 900, then the 4090 really is just a 700U$D gpu for you.

I would say that for games from before 2020, your legendary 9900K shouldn't bottleneck a 4090, but from 2020 onwards...yes, you should expect increasing bottleneck. Spider-Man Remastered is well optimized, but it saturates the PCI interface, therefore it drags an i7 10700K down to even sub-Ryzen 7 3700X (which is weaker than your 9900K) performance, because the intel 10 gen is PCI-E 3 , Zen2 onwards has PCI-E 4. for a GPU as robust as the 4090, this is no longer trivial.

text:
I would just like to point out that the locked FPS test is inherently unfair for GPUs of different performance levels. Power consumption is not linear as you increase clocks and voltage. A faster GPU running at ~50% of its maximum performance is going to be in a much more efficient part of its operating envelope than a slower GPU running at ~90% of its maximum performance.

The RX 6950 XT vs RTX 3090 Ti comparison here is appropriate, but the comparison to the RTX 4090 is not. You can tweak the target FPS to favor different GPUs by changing where they sit in their overall performance/power envelope. (with lower targets generally favoring lower power/lower cost GPUs)

The reality is that each GPU is going to have a performance/W curve based on what % of the maximum performance you are asking for.

text:
I love HUB, it's the first channel I check for reviews, roundups, and comparisons.
So without any critique I want to offer what I hope might be a useful data point. I'd like to explain what I am really interested in seeing when it comes to GPU reviews and especially for next-gen parts.

Perhaps controversially, I'm gradually finding rasterization benchmarks a bit uninteresting. Anything from a 3070 and up can do 4K@60 already and all next-gen GPUs will have more than enough rasterization performance at any resolution.

I'm likely in the minority but last-gen graphics running at framerates beyond what monitors can even support just doesn't hold my attention. Maybe because I'm not a competitive gamer - maybe I'm just ahead of the curve.

The future is unquestionably ray tracing and I feel that's where next-gen GPUs matter. So that's where I'd like to see the focus with a broader suite of RT games being tested.

The RT games tested here were a great mix but left out: The Ascent, Control, Metro EE, Doom Eternal, Deathloop, SpiderMan Remaster,  Resident Evil series, driving games like Dirt 5/Fortza Horizon 5, and even fast paced competitive shooters like Fortnite, Battlefield, and Call of Duty. Lots of different engines and implementations.

There are dozens of RT games on the market today and the days of RT resulting in unplayable framerates are coming to and end. RT testing also gives us a better idea of how these next-gen parts might perform in the near future as RT becomes the default. 

I also feel testing of upscaling features can be left out. I know dropping the internal resolution will net me a linear increase to frame rates. I know any game with upscaling tech can get me 40-80% more frames when enabling the option. That's the result of every DLSS/FSR test ever so there's no surprises or new information to be had. So I'd rather see more games tested.

And DLSS/FSR/XeSS comparisons/tests could be (should be?) independent of the GPU reviews.

Anyhoo, that's my two cents.

text:
15:07 "Truly the first 4K GPU capable of delivering a high refresh gaming experience"
Then there's me who has been running games at 4K120 since the 980Ti (e.g. DOOM 2016 on low settings, but you still get high textures so you're not missing any fine detail, as a 4K experience you're losing almost nothing by running low shadows and reflections).
The GPU benchmarking industry has been screwing with people's expectations of price/performance for basically the entire history of GPU benchmarking. Which is not to say that a GPU benchmark needs to do anything more than compare relative performance from one card to the next, and testing everything at "4K Ultra" does that just fine, it's just when the reviewer makes statements like the quoted example that the review becomes misleading advice instead of just a comparison of processing power.
author: @budthecyborg4575

text:
The reasonable middle ground is obviously we need cards being benchmarked at 4K Medium settings, even though you can still get a lot more optimized than that.
Of course it's impossible for anyone to benchmark a suite of games with all settings min/maxed for the best visual quality at a target framerate, but people need to be aware that custom graphics settings will always net significant performance or visual quality gains over just running a default graphics profile.

text:
Great vid, but to put the new prices in context, I'm typically a $700-$1100 USD GPU buyer, with a a midrange ($400-$500 USD) consumer for my casual PC. The new pricing has turned me into a used GPU buyer. I'm lucky enough to not have been impacted by inflation (yet) as my business almost seems to thrive on it and I'm currently not even accepting new clients. So basically having the money available is not the problem. It's the utter disrespect of the companies involved by constantly raising prices while offering less performance than we should get.

They could literally make two cards above the current 4090 without a problem, and quite often used to. Now they have the 4090 on what was once a 3080 12GB Die, and previous to that was a 1080ti die, a 780 die etc etc. Of course we've also seen Fermi 680's and, of course the GTX 1080 on the 104 die, but that's the only other really outlandish things I've seen Nvidia do. Those cards also weren't $900 USD, nor would they be with inflation. This is just utter idiocy. It would be akin to me telling my existing customers "Tech has just gotten better, and demand for my services is up. Instead of charging $150/hr for on site work I need to charge $275. Yes it's worse value than last year, and prices are down across the board. i also don't have to pay a 25% fee to the government (ei the tariffs that were lifted on GPU exports from China)...basically I just want more money."

The customers would essentially have a decision to make when renewing their contracts; get a lesser quality experience from a chain company like Best Buy's "Geek Squad" (who do fine work mind you, but often take longer, may not be experienced with, idk, antique Cisco networks. Or they can pay far more for someone who specializes in each issue that may arise. In addition, they can also suck it up and pay the extra money, taking it away from money they'd otherwise reinvest in their own businesses, or other small businesses for that matter. I suppose it's the morality of the whole thing.

Luckily for consumers, when Nvidia does this there are a few other options. Whether that's buying an AMD card or a used Nvidia card from the previous generation. It certainly leaves a sour taste in my mouth though. Knowing what I am willing to spend is enough to buy a beater first car for a 16/yo that you can work on together, maybe change the radiator, fix the exhaust and teach the kid how to drive stick; or buy a not top of the line gaming GPU for $1100 bucks because that just doesn't cut it anymore. In fact, it will be about 40% less powerful than the current NOT fastest GPU they are releasing if you go that route, and probably only about 10% faster than an $800 card...if I'm willing to bump my price up $100 bucks? Nah, call me naive, but the principle of the whole thing really bothers me.

Prices have come down on everything but the chips over the last 12 months. EVERYTHING. Even shipping is down a bit. Then you factor in their no longer needing to pay the 25% China import tariffs and Nvidia is being beyond greedy. A 67% profit margin, down from 70% the previous 4 quarters is bloody obscene, and something we really need to put our foot down about. No, I don't pocket a million dollars a year after taxes (not including investments which I don't plan on spending for another 20 or 30 years...or at least until I retire)., but I make more than enough, my house is paid off, I don't have any Car payments save insurance, my phones are paid for so there's no recurring bill there and I don't carry credit card debt more than a month + 1 day. And they've turned me into a used market shopper, even though gaming is my main hobby, taking up about 21 hours/wk of my time.

Wish them luck (bad), as if they can move someone like myself away from the new market I can't see these cards selling all that well at $1600+ after two weeks on the market.

text:
@DDHDTV  Yeah you’re right A 4K monitor doesn’t change the gaming experience as much as gaming in a 4K OLED TV does ! in fact gaming in 4K OLED at Ultra max settings smooth FPS is complete eye candy & i think nothing compliments The Power of the GPU & the incredible details in graphics in modern games than a 4K OLED for gaming & content consumption ( like 42” LG C2 for example ) 

With that said it’s true 4K gaming at the highest settings still requires a lot of Hardware Beef , We need much powerful GPU CPU & Power output to play true 4K Ray tracing ultra settings ( upcoming games will be too demanding )

also a OLED should not used for static content & regular desktop usages as it may have pixel burn in issues . so we need Dual screen set up to eliminate the risk with a 4K TV & a crisp 2K monitor ( not to mention the $$$$s we need to spend for the dream 4K Hardware ) 

4K OLED is definitely a huge jump in PC gaming experience but there’s still time , may be at the end of 2023 with GPU’s like RTX 4090 Ti | Radeon RX7950 XTX | Radeon RX7990XTX with Ryzen 7950x3D it will be possible ! 

PS: I don’t consider AI frame generation like DLSS & FSR as a pinnacle , it isn’t  the advanced settings tbh , it’s not the true Ultra max . it just generates a Fake frame in-order make it appear smooth for us ! that’s not to be considered as a real frame rate , so until we achieve that feat of at-least averaging 60FPS Ray tracing & Ultra settings , We’re not truly Ray tracing or 4K except for a few old titles .

It's by no means a perfect rule of thumb how where Nvidia has gone to the heterogeneous CUDA core layout and AMD is using Infinity cache. So for Nvidia they're on the lower end of the scale and AMD is on the higher end of the scale, while the opposite is true when you go down in resolution (obviously).

But it's good enough to get a ballpark idea, and given the 4K numbers here, it's quite obvious that you'll get above 60FPS at 8k. But it's also clear that you're back to needing upscaling if you want RT cranked up.

Now personally I can only barely detect the difference between 1440p and 4k on a 27" monitor, so who and why someone would want 8k is another question entirely.

Cost comparisons do not make sense without including inflation. If you'd adjust prices of previous generations for inflation, the 4090 is not more expensive than the 3090Ti or 3090 and just slightly more expensive than both Pascal Titan cards. In fact even the 2080Ti is only 185USD cheaper.

And concerning power consumption. Der8auer has a very interesting chapter in his test in which he tested out the effect of an adjusted power target on performance. At 60-70% the performance was less than 10% lower but you'd save 1/3 of the power consumption. We have to conclude: NVIDIA probably realized that after moving to TSMC from Samsung their cooling solutions were massively oversized and that they calculated with way too much power draw (which led to further adopting the stupid new power connector). A 4090 with a TDP of 350W would still have been a massive performance beast and could have been fed with 2x 8-Pin power connectors (2x 150W) + PCIe slot (max 75W).

text: @drago939393  I refer to it as "RAM" rather than "VRAM" because in compute you are using it as such.
author: @LAG09

text: @LAG09  I get that, I was asking how the (V)RAM works for neural/AI things.
author: @drago939393

text: @drago939393  It allows you to work on bigger or more dense datasets resulting in higher quality output.
author: @LAG09

text: @LAG09  Hm, how does regular RAM factor into it?
author: @drago939393

text:
​ @drago939393  The system RAM? GPUs can't access it directly and hence its so slow as to be un-usable mid-computation. The general way to write performant GPU code is to load up all the data you need into GPU memory, run the GPU code, read back to system RAM, write some more into GPU memory, run the GPU code again, rinse and repeat until you're done.

To write really performant GPU code you write it to be aware of the cache to use and fit the most often used values into them. You can't make it explicit, but you can give NVCC (Nvidia's CUDA compiler) very strong suggestions with keywords.

text:
Sounds to me like the 4090 is unable to keep itself fed for 1440p at all, hence the generally low scores at 1440p and 1080p, but leaping ahead, again generally, for 4k. A bit like the E cores on the 12900K, unable to use those cores except on trivially parallel tasks. So UNLESS you have a high refresh 4K monitor the 4090 is not to be bought, because the 4090 just fails to feed itself at less than that. See the cases where DLSS don't improve FPS for cases where even "4K" it cannot keep itself fed, so it doesn't see a gain at DLSS doing "4k" compared to native 4K, with ray tracing.
I would also consider that one reason why the 4090 was so efficient at 90FPS and 1440p was because most of the card was idle and utterly unused, whereas the 3090 and 6950 were not capped at that, they were mostly working, while the 4090 was often idle in many parts of the die, so that isn't a usable case when intercomparisons, your test would only be valid as a test between the 4090 and the top (ish) Navi31, where theoretically they are both as unworried as each other at 90FPS and 1440p. The test you did was more comparing the 3090 to the 6950, both being "roughly" as sweating as each other.
In short, if you are working a 60Hz 4K monitor, you can't really justify the price of the 4090, and if you want 1440p or 1080p then you are not going to get anything other than an underclock for a high high price, so you would be better off using, say, the 4070 or maybe one of the 4080s, for that, because perhaps those can keep themselves fed at 1440p, so doing just as well as the 4090 at those resolutions for a heck of a lot less money.

text:
@karlhungus545  Because DSR is a thing? You can upscale a 1080p resolution to 4k and than display the 4k frame as a 1080p image on a 1080p monitor. The resulting image is thus significantly less aliased. 

This is essentially supersampling and although the upscaled image does not have the same quality as native 4k, it is still vastly superior to native 1080p. So yes, even people with 1080p monitors can benefit from 4k GPU's.

text:
​ @leonro  

Then read again buddy, as you are wrong.

"But definitely not 4k 240hz"

You are not reading what i'm writing. Yes it is possible VIA DSC(!) (close to loss-less compression technology) which supports up to 240Hz @ 4K via HDMI 2.1.

"and there already are Samsung monitors that do just that."

Ehm yes? That's exactly what i'm trying to tell you. Look up the HDMI specs of these, they are almost all HDMI 2.1. Take the SAMSUNG ODYSSEY NEO G7 for example. A 4K/165 Hz monitor with "only" HDMI 2.1 and DP 1.4. Or even the NEO G8 with it's 240Hz's. You guessed it: Display Port 1.4 and HDMI 2.1.

"Also, you wouldn't want to do 8-bit colour if your display is capable of 10-bit imo"

It's not a question about "what you wouldn't want", but what's possible due to bandwith restrictions. You are forced to sacrifice quality (live with 8 bit vs. the 10 bit) when compressing via DSC in order to reach up to 240Hz. But none the less it's possible/supported like i stated from the get go.

It's all documented. Look into it again:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HDMI#Refresh_frequency_limits_for_standard_video

https://www.tomshardware.com/features/displayport-vs-hdmi-better-for-gaming

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2022/01/samsung-brings-240-hz-refresh-rates-to-4k-monitors/

text:
@haukionkannel  I'm not saying that they CAN'T, I'm just wondering if they WON'T. Those are two completely different things.

Your argument held a lot more water with the RTX 30. The 3090 was a lot more exclusive than the 4090 is. Most 1440p gamers could just buy the 3080 for 700$. Whereas now, no one wants to buy the 4080 for 1200$, so they may just skip it and buy the 4090 instead.

Also, Nvidia has specifically increased the production of the 4090 by a LOT (compared to the 3090). So they're CLEARLY trying to push the 4090 to a broader audience. And my argument is this: the broader audience DOES NOT have a high refresh 4k display that would make a proper use of this card. Will SOME of those people buy 4k high refresh monitors? Possibly, but those monitors also cost an arm and a leg to buy, on top of the already expensive GPU. 

You can't squeeze people that would typically pay 800-1000$ for a GPU, finesse them into paying 1600$ for a GPU, and THEN ON TOP OF IT, force them to buy a 4k high refresh rate monitor as well - just to get the most performance out of it! This is what I'm saying: the value proposition is nonsensical.

A lot of 1440p gamers may be tempted to just buy the 4090 (instead of the 4080, which is absolutely terrible), when in reality this card doesn't really suit that resolution very well. That's all I'm saying, it's a warning. Each use case is going to be its own case, of course.

text:
You're making a conceptual mistake here when you speak of the "DLSS bottleneck". It's not DLSS that's bottlenecking the GPU in those RT tests where DLSS results and non-DLSS results are the same, but the CPU.
Ray Tracing requires the CPU to build the tree like structure that then the RT units will traverse in order to compute a ray hitting the mesh, so in those scenarios where the 4090 performs at native as good as with DLSS 2 is just because the CPU can't even feed the 4090 at the limit of it's capabilities when native, so generating frames with lower resolution changes nothing.
The 4090 has those new RT cores with the fancy micro-mesh feature that should allow to eliminate (or at least greatly reduce) this bottleneck, but that would require specific programming on the developer's side so it's not having an effect on those games.

text:
Something really disastrous would have to happen for the 4090 to not lose badly to AMD.  There's no real process advantage - 4N is just a slightly tweaked 5N, and AMD's 5N is already tweaked from the standard 5N.  You're also greatly overestimating the difference between Samsung's 8nm node and TSMC's 7nm node.

Compared to the 3090 Ti, the 4090 has 52% more shaders, and 36% higher clock speeds.  Combined, that's 107% faster overall.  But it's only managing 60% on average in GPU-bound scenarios.

Compared to the 6950 XT, the top Navi 31 card (7950 XT, perhaps) has 140% more shaders.  We don't know clock speeds, so let's just assume they haven't changed.  Perfect scaling would make that card 40% faster than the 4090.  If you assume the same relative scaling as the 4090 got, it'd still be at least 10% ahead.  That's without any clock speed increases.

text:
AFAIK there is no indication that the AD104 die is cut down in the 12GB 4080; the "real" 4080 has its own AD103 design and is a larger physical die size.  But taking that into consideration, its almost worse; for some perspective, AD104 is a smaller die size than the 6700s, and barely larger than the GA106 used in the 3060 or even the TU116 used in the 1660s, and all use a 192bit memory bus...so from that perspective the 12GB 4080 feels like its more of a 60 series than even a 70, let alone 80.

Then there's AD103 in the "real" 4080, and even that is a smaller die size compared to GA104 in the 3070, each also working with a 256bit bus...

The only saving grace for nVidia is if performance is actually there, and considering even the 12GB 4080 packs more transistors than the 3090Ti (for perspective, the 3070 has fewer transistors than the 2080Ti) they might just be able to pull it off, but they really never should have called it a 4080, even if performance is there
